terms.definition: The moment when the score is computed and acted on. Only information known at that moment may enter the model.

A variable that carries information from after the prediction time. It makes a model look better on past data than it can be in use. For example, the duration of the last call to a client is known only once the call has ended, so a model that uses it to decide whom to call relies on information it cannot have before the call; it looks excellent on past calls and is useless in a campaign.
Whether a variable is known at the prediction time. It is a decision about the use case, not a property the data can prove.
Rows held apart from model fitting and used to compare models and choose a policy. Once used to choose, they are no longer independent evidence.

How the values of one column spread over the rows, read as how often each value occurs or, for a measurement, its range, quartiles, and missing cells. Read on training rows only, it leaves the validation rows unexplored.
An outcome that occurs in a small share of the rows. A model can then look accurate by predicting the common outcome everywhere, so it is judged against the base rate.

The share of rows with the positive outcome. Any model must be compared with what this share alone would give. For example, when few clients subscribe a term deposit, a model that predicts "no" for everyone is right for most clients and finds no subscriber; the base rate is the bar any call list must beat.

The simplest reference model, a constant score equal to the training base rate. Keeping the baseline is a valid conclusion.

terms.definition: A model that turns a weighted sum of the features into a score between zero and one. It ranks rows; its scores are not calibrated probabilities unless that is checked.
The number a model gives to each row to rank it. A higher score places the row earlier in the queue.
The rule that turns scores into actions, either a threshold on the score or a fixed capacity of rows to act on.
Act on every row whose score is at least the threshold. The number of actions then depends on the data.

terms.definition: How many rows the policy acts on, also shown as a share of the partition.
Rows with exactly the score at the cut-off. They are counted pro rata, as an expected value, rather than broken arbitrarily.
Resampling the same validation rows for both policies at once, so the interval describes their difference rather than each one separately.

The difference between two models measured on the same rows, such as the logistic model's precision minus the baseline's at one rule. Pairing removes the noise of which rows each model was measured on.

A range that shows how much a figure could move if other rows had been drawn. In this study it is a percentile interval of the paired bootstrap, so it describes the variability of these validation rows, not a guaranteed range for a future campaign. For example, a precision interval that runs from close to the base rate to well above it says that the call list may barely beat calling clients at random.

terms.definition: The range between two percentiles of the bootstrap replicates. It shows sampling variability on these rows, not the performance of a future campaign.
Choosing a model, a threshold, or a capacity by looking at validation results. The chosen figures are optimistic for that reason.
A statement backed by the dataset documentation, with its source.
A statement the scenario takes as given without evidence. It can be challenged and is never a decision.
A choice recorded with the user's own words in reply to a restatement. The engine records the words; it cannot verify who typed them.
A restated choice waiting for the user's answer. It is not a decision until it is confirmed.
A result computed under decisions that have since changed. It is kept for the record but is not cited.

The chance that a randomly drawn positive row gets a higher score than a randomly drawn negative row. It judges the ranking over every possible cut-off, not the result of one decision rule. For example, for a campaign that ranks clients before calling them about a term deposit, an AUC of one half means the ranking puts subscribers ahead of non-subscribers no better than chance.

The precision reached each time the ranked list meets a positive row, averaged from the top of the list down. Unlike the AUC, it depends on the base rate, so it suits a rare outcome. For example, when few clients subscribe, average precision tells how pure the top of the call list stays, which is what the calling team feels.

The precision of the rows acted on divided by the base rate. A lift above one means the rule finds positive rows more often than acting at random would. For example, if the clients called first subscribe twice as often as the clients in general, the lift of that call list is two.

Whether a score matches how often the outcome occurs among rows with that score. A model can rank well and still be badly calibrated, and this study does not assess calibration. For example, if the clients a model scores at about one in five subscribe far less often than one in five, its scores cannot be read as probabilities, even if the ranking is useful.

A model that fits the noise of its training rows as well as their pattern. It looks better on the rows it was fitted on than on new rows. For example, a model that memorises which months of the training clients had many subscriptions can score those clients well and the next campaign badly; the gap between training and validation figures reveals it.

A penalty on large model weights during fitting. It trades a little fit on the training rows for steadier predictions on new rows. For example, in a logistic model of client subscriptions with many job and month categories, regularisation keeps a rare category from getting an extreme weight from a handful of clients.

Turning a category column into one indicator column per category, set for the rows that have that category. A linear model needs it because categories have no order. For example, the job of a client becomes one indicator per job, such as "technician" or "retired", and the model learns a weight for each.

Filling a missing value with a substitute, such as the median of the training rows, before fitting. The substitute is computed on training rows only, and an indicator can record that the value was missing. For example, a client whose account balance is missing would get the median balance of the training clients, never a figure computed with validation clients.

Rescaling a numeric column to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one, with both computed on training rows. It puts features on one scale, so their weights and a penalty treat them alike. For example, a client's age in years and account balance in euros are rescaled so that the weight on balance is not tiny only because euro amounts are large numbers.

Dividing the development rows into several folds, fitting on all folds but one and measuring on the one left out, in turn. Every development row is measured once, so the estimate rests on more rows than one validation partition; a choice made with it is still optimistic. For example, with five folds of the clients, each model is fitted five times and judged each time on clients it did not see.

Rows set apart and sealed before any look at the data, opened once, after the model and the decision rule are frozen, to measure them on rows that played no part in any choice. It is the study's only independent evidence. For example, the clients sealed at the start are scored once by the chosen model and call list; any change made after that opening is reported as made after the final test.

Every row outside the sealed final test, the rows the study may explore, split into training and validation rows, and use to choose. What they show is development evidence, not final evidence. For example, the clients in the development rows feed the exploration, the model fits, and the comparison of call lists, while the sealed clients stay unread.

An interval for a proportion, such as a positive rate in a group, that stays inside zero and one and remains sensible for small groups and rates close to zero. It shows how much the rate could move with another sample of the same size. For example, a rate computed on a few dozen clients gets a wide interval, the same rate on a thousand clients a narrow one.

The range of a chart's figures after shuffling the outcome among the training rows several times with a fixed seed, which breaks any real link between the variable and the outcome. A pattern that stays inside the band is what chance alone draws; one above every shuffle is unlikely to be chance alone. For example, if the rates by job group differ less than they do after shuffling who subscribed, the differences are not evidence of anything.

A decision chosen after looking at the outcome in the data. It is allowed, but it is recorded with the analyses that motivated it, because a choice adapted to the training rows makes the validation figures slightly optimistic. For example, capping a variable because a chart of the outcome looked odd at its extremes is a data-contingent preparation.

The smallest gain over the baseline that would make the model worth adopting, fixed before any model is fitted, so the result cannot move the bar. The conclusion is read against it. For example, deciding before the models that the call list must beat the baseline's precision by a given number of points, and keeping the baseline when it does not.

How well one variable alone predicts the outcome, measured out of fold on the training rows. A variable that predicts far better than the others raises a question about when its value becomes known, because a value recorded at or after the outcome would leak it. It never decides which variables to keep. For example, the length of the last call predicts the answer of that call very well, because it is only known once the call has ended.

Missing-value indicators, the minimum rows of a category, caps at training quantiles, and log transforms are learnt on training rows only and applied unchanged to the validation rows. The default changes nothing.

Baseline
A constant baseline and a logistic model are fitted on training rows and scored on validation rows.
Predictions on validation rows are stored, so a new policy never requires a refit.
The comparison is made on validation rows, which are then no longer independent evidence.
The policy step reads these stored predictions.
Decision policy
The intended use is: Teaching simulation: prioritize contacts when call capacity is limited. A policy turns scores into a number of actions the team can handle.
Each rule is evaluated on the stored validation predictions, with ties at the cut counted pro rata and paired bootstrap intervals.
The figures describe these validation rows after a choice made on them; they are optimistic and are not a forecast.
Adopting a different threshold or capacity recomputes the evaluation without refitting any model.
Confirmed decision
The conclusion says what can be claimed, for which use, and with which limits.
You choose a verdict and write the text; keeping the baseline or calling the study inconclusive are valid results.
The conclusion rests on validation rows that were used for selection.
The limits listed under "What is not yet defensible" stay attached to it.
